extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, instructors, and math-education researchers (graduate students and teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: A framework for evaluating and diagnosing mathematical problem-solving performance (solutions, not just proofs) using Schoenfeld's four-component model: resources, heuristics, control (metacognition), and belief systems. Useful for grading student solutions and coaching problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositional and procedural knowledge available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes definitions, theorems, formulas, algorithms; worked examples in long-term memory; routine subroutines (factoring, integration by parts). Evaluate whether the solver had the necessary factual and procedural knowledge and whether those resources were accessible and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pólya-style strategies for moving when stuck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical heuristics to look for or expect: look for analogous problems; specialize/generalize; work backwards from the goal; draw a figure; decompose the problem; consider an auxiliary problem; vary the problem. Assess whether appropriate heuristic strategies were chosen and applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (Metacognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisions that orchestrate the use of resources and heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metacognitive actions such as when to switch strategies; how long to pursue an approach before abandoning it; monitoring progress (are we closer to the goal?); resource allocation across sub-problems; and reflection after solution. This dimension judges the student's orchestration and regulation of problem-solving activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The implicit 'world view' the solver brings to the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes orientations like: math is a coherent body of ideas (vs. a set of disconnected tricks); problems should be approached by understanding (vs. by template-matching); a real problem takes time (not 5 minutes); solutions can be checked, generalized, and reflected on. Evaluate whether the solver's beliefs supported productive problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic classification for failed attempts (R/H/C/B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any failed problem-solving attempt, classify the failure as R, H, C, or B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R — missing the resource; H — had the resource, didn't think to use it; C — used it but didn't notice the dead end / didn't allocate time; B — gave up because of belief that it was unsolvable. Use these codes to pinpoint where breakdowns occurred (knowledge, strategic choice, metacognition, or beliefs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good solution criterion: Correct resources used appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good solution' exhibits correct resources used appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When grading, check that the solver used relevant definitions, theorems, formulas, or algorithms and applied them correctly and at the appropriate points in the solution, rather than invoking inappropriate facts or irrelevant procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good solution criterion: Heuristic choice visibly justified
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good solution' shows that the heuristic choice is visibly justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should make evident why a chosen strategy was selected (e.g., why specializing, generalizing, or working backwards was promising). Solutions should include indication of strategic thinking, not just end computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good solution criterion: Control — abandoned dead ends honestly described
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good solution' displays control: abandoned dead ends are honestly described, not airbrushed; time is spent on the genuinely hard step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should look for evidence of monitoring and control: acknowledgment of approaches that failed, rationale for abandoning them, and concentrated effort on the non-routine core rather than polishing trivial steps to hide gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good solution criterion: Reflection — alternative approaches and generalizations discussed
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good solution' includes reflection: after the solution, alternative approaches and generalizations are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the student reflects on the solution by suggesting other methods, checking the result, generalizing the argument, or commenting on the method's scope and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom protocol diagnostic: ability to articulate reasoning under interruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Schoenfeld's classroom protocol: interrupt students mid-problem with 'What exactly are you doing?', 'Why are you doing that?', 'How does it help you?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these questions to test whether a student is solving by reflex or by reasoning. A student who cannot answer is likely relying on rote or reflexive procedures rather than consciously controlled problem solving. This serves as an in-situ diagnostic of control and understanding.
